paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The Lorentz force is the force that electric and magnetic fields exert on a charged particle. It decides how charged particles move wherever such fields are present. That makes it the basis of many things, from electric motors and particle accelerators to the way plasmas behave. The force has two parts, one from each kind of field.

paragraphs.heading: Two parts
paragraphs.text: The electric part, written qE, pushes along the electric field for a positive charge and against it for a negative one. It tends to speed the particle up along a straight line. The magnetic part, written q(v × B), acts at right angles both to the magnetic field and to the way the particle is moving. It bends the particle's path into a curve, often a circle or a helix. To find its direction for a positive charge, use the right-hand rule: point your index finger along the velocity and your middle finger along the field, and your thumb shows the force.

paragraphs.heading: Circles and drifts
paragraphs.text: In a uniform magnetic field, the sideways push sends particles around in circles or helices, which is called cyclotron motion. In a plasma, the motion of electrons or ions can often be pictured as two pieces added together: a fairly fast circle around a point called the guiding center, and a slower drift of that point. Different kinds of particles can drift at different speeds, depending on their charge, mass or temperature. Those differences can produce electric currents or pull chemicals apart.

paragraphs.heading: The magnetic part does no work
paragraphs.text: Here is a surprising consequence. The magnetic force changes which way a particle travels, but it does no mechanical work on it. The rate at which the field passes energy to the particle is the dot product of velocity and force, which works out to 𝐯⋅𝐅 = q 𝐯⋅𝐄. The magnetic term drops out because any vector is perpendicular to its cross product with another vector. So only the electric field can add energy to a particle or take it away, changing its kinetic energy.

paragraphs.heading: The push on a wire
paragraphs.text: The same idea explains the push on a current-carrying wire sitting in a magnetic field, sometimes called the Laplace force. Each moving charge in the wire feels the Lorentz force, and together these add up to a net force on the wire. For a straight, stationary wire in a uniform field, the force is 𝐅 = Iℓ × 𝐁. Here I is the current, and ℓ points along the wire in the direction of the current, with a size equal to the wire's length. A related version covers the electromotive force that appears in a wire loop as it moves through a magnetic field, as in Faraday's law of induction.

paragraphs.heading: Defining the fields
paragraphs.text: Some textbooks turn the law around and use it to define the electric and magnetic fields. In that view, E and B at a point are fixed by the force that a test particle, with charge q and velocity v, would feel at that point, even when no charge is actually present. This works even for particles moving close to the speed of light. Not everyone agrees, though, that it is the most fundamental way to define the fields.

paragraphs.heading: History and limits
paragraphs.text: Together with Maxwell's equations, which say how charges and currents create electric and magnetic fields, the Lorentz force law is the foundation of classical electrodynamics. Historians suggest the law is already implicit in an 1865 paper by James Clerk Maxwell. Oliver Heaviside correctly worked out the magnetic part, and a few years later, in 1895, Hendrik Lorentz gave a complete derivation that added the electric part. The law still holds in special relativity, but it breaks down at small scales where quantum effects matter; the intrinsic spin of particles, for example, brings extra interactions it leaves out.
